The Argentinian silverside Odontesthes bonariensis exhibits a maximum recorded total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger atherinopsid species in South American freshwater systems. Field surveys across the Pampean region indicate that individuals approaching this asymptotic length are relatively uncommon, as most captures consist of fish between 25 and 35 centimeters. This species is highly valued in recreational fisheries and aquaculture operations throughout its native range, which includes the lagunas and lower reaches of the Río de la Plata basin. The largest specimens are typically slow-growing females that have avoided intensive fishing pressure, and their size is often associated with advanced age and substantial lipid reserves accumulated over multiple growing seasons. Such individuals can attain considerable body mass, with the ultimate wet weight recorded at 963 grams [Wwi = 963 grams] based on morphometric relationships derived from extensive sampling. This mass reflects the substantial somatic investment required to reach the upper end of the size distribution in a temperate, seasonally productive environment.

Reproductive development in Odontesthes bonariensis is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age alone, with puberty occurring once individuals reach a total length of 13.2 centimeters [Lp = 13.2 centimeters]. At this threshold, corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 17.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 17.5 grams], the gonads begin active gametogenesis and the fish become capable of participating in spawning aggregations. This size-based maturation schedule is common among iteroparous temperate silversides, where winter resource accumulation plays a critical role in determining whether an individual will mature during the subsequent spring. The length at puberty is notably small relative to the species' ultimate size, indicating a life history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive entry over extended somatic growth. Juveniles that attain this size by their first autumn are often observed with developing gonads, whereas smaller conspecifics delay maturation until the following year. This flexibility allows the population to buffer against interannual variation in growing season length and food availability.

At a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a thermal regime typical of spring spawning conditions in the shallow lakes of Buenos Aires Province, reproductive output reaches its maximum expression. The daily reproduction rate at this temperature has been documented as approximately 153 eggs per female per day [Ri = approximately 153 eggs per female per day], a value derived from the species' relative fecundity of roughly 58,483 eggs per kilogram of female body mass. This high fecundity is characteristic of pelagic-egg spawners that provide no parental care, relying instead on numerical output to offset substantial egg and larval mortality. The rate can be partitioned into discrete spawning events, with individual females releasing several thousand eggs per batch and spawning repeatedly over a protracted breeding season that can extend from late winter through early summer. The thermal dependence of this reproductive rate is pronounced, as metabolic and gonadal processes slow considerably below 14 °C and become energetically constrained above 24 °C.

Neonatal mass in this species is remarkably small, reflecting the production of numerous tiny pelagic eggs. The wet weight at birth is just 0.0021 grams [Wwb = 0.0021 grams], corresponding to an egg diameter of approximately 1.6 millimeters that yields a prolarva weighing only a few milligrams upon chorion rupture. This minimal initial mass represents a classic example of the fecundity-versus-offspring-size trade-off, where the energetic investment per zygote is minimized to maximize total egg output. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is endotrophic for the first several days, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before mouth opening and the onset of first exogenous feeding. During this lecithotrophic phase, the larva remains largely motionless near the water surface, absorbing yolk and completing organogenesis of the digestive tract and visual system. The small size at hatching makes the prolarvae highly vulnerable to starvation if exogenous prey items are not available at the point of no return, which typically occurs between four and six days post-eclosion at 17 °C.

Longevity in Odontesthes bonariensis is moderate for a freshwater teleost of its ultimate size, with life span reaching 10 years [am = 10 years] when individuals experience the thermal conditions of their native habitat at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This maximum documented age has been derived from otolith annulus counts in populations from relatively stable lacustrine environments where fishing mortality is low. The species displays a Type III survivorship curve, with extremely high mortality during the early larval stages followed by progressively declining death rates among juveniles and adults. Senescence becomes apparent after approximately seven or eight years, with older fish showing reduced reproductive output and increased incidence of parasitic infections. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Odontesthes argentinensis suggest that the life span of O. bonariensis is near the upper limit for the genus, likely facilitated by its temperate, relatively cool-water distribution. Trade-offs between early maturity, high fecundity, and moderate longevity are consistent with a ruderal life history strategy adapted to productive but seasonally variable environments.
